title: the WSG infravision and Table 41 slice - the heat-vision definition with the 60/30/120 infravisual ranges and the outdoor range of normal vision grid, printed p. 73
audit_comment: The infravision and Table 41 rules: infravision, or heat vision, is the ability to see the shapes of objects by sensing radiation in the infrared spectrum; all nonhuman player characters have it, most out to 60 yards (outdoor scale); halflings other than pure-blooded Stouts see 30 yards; drow, duergar and deep gnomes see 120. Table 41 gives the outdoor range of normal vision in yards for six conditions across four light levels: clear 500/300/50/25; overcast 400/250/50/25; moderate fog 150/100/25/15; heavy fog, rain or snow 50/30/15/10; heavy snow with wind 35/25/10/5; blowing sand or dust 20/20/10/5. The given range is the distance at which a viewer discerns a size M object that stands out from the terrain; double it for size L, halve it for size S. The range assumes long-range concentration and a target that is not concealed: the orc lying down on the plain is greatly harder to spot, and prone in three-foot grass it is effectively invisible until the viewer is very close. In daylight or twilight a character can scan long and short range at once by shifting his gaze every few seconds, even at full speed; in moonlight or darkness that fails - a moving character may step into a crevasse he just looked at, so a lone traveler watches his footing, a group splits lookout duty, and stopping to peer is safest but still no guard against a nearby silent moving hazard.

The chapter frame: as many as three visual senses -
normal vision, infravision, ultravision - each with
advantages in some situations. The definition: normal
vision is what humans and most creatures use most of the
time, seeing images and colors within the visible
spectrum between infrared and ultraviolet. The ranges:
in clear air during daylight the effective range is 500
yards (size M recognized by basic form), size S visible
from 250, size L from at least 1000 - or much greater
for a dragon or a tall building. The obstruction and
elevation semantics: anything in the line of sight
obstructs, ideal conditions are rare at shared ground
elevation; the worked example - a six-foot orc on a
flat plain visible at 500 yards drops to 250 (as if
size S) under three-foot grass because only half its
body shows; a lone mountain peak sees for miles but
the range is unchanged - still within 500 yards of a
size M to identify it; the converse: the man on the
peak is himself recognizable within 500 - long-range
visibility a blessing and a curse at once. THE SETTLE:
two-way clean on the first pass - both readers agree on
every number (the 500/250/1000, the three senses, the
six-foot orc, the three-foot grass); the pdfy header
line reads VIS1, a running-head artifact, not content.
